title: Messi Faces Backlash for Trying to Get Cucurella Sent Off in World Cup Final
excerpt: Argentina captain Lionel Messi drew widespread criticism after attempting to exploit FIFA's mouth-covering rule to get Spain's Marc Cucurella red-carded during the 2026 World Cup final, which Spain won 1-0 in extra time.
body:
• Lionel Messi attempted to get Spain defender Marc Cucurella sent off for briefly covering his mouth during the 2026 World Cup final, drawing widespread criticism from pundits and fans.
  • The incident occurred seconds after Argentina's Enzo Fernandez was shown a red card for a reckless challenge on Pau Cubarsi in stoppage time.
  • Referee Slavko Vincic declined to act because FIFA's "Prestianni rule" requires evidence of a hostile confrontation — and Cucurella's brief gesture was deemed non-confrontational.
  • Spain went on to win the final 1-0 in extra time through a Ferran Torres goal in the 105th minute, with Argentina failing to register a single shot on target across 120 minutes.

What Happened Between Messi and Cucurella

Sunday's 2026 FIFA World Cup final at MetLife Stadium was heading for extra time when the match turned ugly. In stoppage time at the end of the second half, Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez — already booked for dissent — lunged into a reckless challenge on Barcelona's teenage defender Pau Cubarsi. Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic had no choice but to show a second yellow card, reducing Argentina to 10 men.

What followed was chaos. Argentine players swarmed Vincic in protest. In the midst of the melee, Spain left-back Marc Cucurella approached Messi and began speaking. As he did so, Cucurella briefly touched his mouth with his hand — a gesture that, under FIFA's new rule introduced specifically for this tournament, can result in an automatic red card.

Messi seized on the moment immediately. The 39-year-old captain raised his hand, waved frantically at the referee, and pointed directly at Cucurella, clearly demanding the Spaniard be expelled. Vincic was unmoved. Play continued, and Cucurella stayed on the pitch.

The 'Prestianni Rule' and Why Cucurella Was Not Sent Off

FIFA's mouth-covering rule — widely known as the "Prestianni rule" — was introduced ahead of the 2026 World Cup following a controversy in last season's Champions League. Benfica midfielder Gianluca Prestianni was accused of directing homophobic abuse at Real Madrid's Vinícius Júnior during a knockout match, covering his mouth to conceal his words from cameras. Prestianni received a six-game ban from UEFA.

In response, FIFA announced that players covering their mouths during confrontations would face automatic red cards at the World Cup. The rule was enforced early in the tournament: Paraguay's Miguel Almirón became the first player sent off under it, and Ecuador's Piero Hincapié was dismissed for a similar offence during a Round of 32 defeat to Mexico.

But the rule's wording contains a crucial qualifier. A red card applies only when a player covers their mouth during a confrontation, with evidence of hostile intent. A review of match footage showed Cucurella walking calmly toward Messi, briefly touching his mouth while speaking, with no obvious malice. There was nothing to suggest a heated exchange, according to Sports Illustrated. With no evidence of confrontational behaviour, Cucurella was given the benefit of the doubt.

"It is desperation. Argentina play like that, we know that's what they do. The one thing you want is good sportsmanship. That was sad to see, Lionel Messi doing that."

— Wayne Rooney, BBC Sport

Pundits and Fans Turn on Messi

The criticism was swift and unsparing. Former England captain Wayne Rooney, working as a BBC pundit, called Messi's actions "desperation" and said it was "sad to see." Fellow BBC analyst Joe Hart was equally blunt: "I didn't enjoy that at all from Lionel Messi. You realise how on top Spain are if even Lionel Messi is reverting to that."

On ITV, former Arsenal defender Lee Dixon went further, calling Messi "a baby" for trying to get an opponent dismissed. "You shouldn't be such a baby to try and get someone sent off for that; it's ridiculous," Dixon said on air. TalkSPORT commentator Jim Proudfoot described Messi as "not happy" that Cucurella had approached an Argentine player "with his mouth covered," noting that Messi argued it should have been deemed confrontational under the letter of the law.

BBC presenter Gabby Logan described the moment as "desperation from Messi," while former Manchester City goalkeeper Micah Richards offered a partial defence: "There's not much in that. He's not got his full hand over, it was half wasn't it? You don't want to see people getting sent off in a World Cup final for that."

On social media, the backlash was even more severe. Fans called Messi's behaviour "shameful" and a "disgrace," with many arguing that it shattered his long-cultivated image as football's quiet gentleman.

A Bitter End to Messi's World Cup Career

The incident added a sour footnote to what was almost certainly Messi's final World Cup match. Argentina's 1-0 defeat — sealed by Ferran Torres's strike in the 106th minute of extra time — was a thorough undoing of the defending champions. Spain dominated the entire contest, with Argentina failing to produce a single shot on target across 120 minutes of football.

For Indian football fans who have idolised Messi across two decades, the final was a deflating farewell. The image of the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner frantically gesturing at a referee to get an opponent expelled sits uneasily alongside the tearful celebrations of Qatar 2022.

What This Means for the Mouth-Covering Rule

The Cucurella incident has reignited debate about the rule's clarity. The subjectivity of what constitutes a "confrontation" leaves the door open for gamesmanship — precisely the kind Messi attempted. UEFA has already announced it will take a different approach, using yellow cards for "attempting to conceal communication as an act of unsporting behaviour" rather than automatic reds.

Whether FIFA retains its stricter version for future tournaments remains to be seen. The rule's intent — preventing covert abuse — is widely supported. Its enforcement, as the World Cup final demonstrated, remains a work in progress.
